item.title: Small Nations Chess Association restarts activities and elects new Board
item.dc:creator: editor_d
item.description: Members of the Small Nations Chess Association (SNACA) convened in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, for the Association’s General Assembly, where they agreed to revitalize SNACA’s operations, approved new statutes, and elected a new Board to serve a two-year term. SNACA now includes 35 member federations from four continents, reflecting the growing international community of chess federations represented within the Association. As part of its renewed agenda, SNACA is planning to organize its first individual championship in 2027, marking an important milestone in the Association’s development and future activities. The General Assembly in Samarkand represents a new chapter for SNACA as it continues to strengthen cooperation among small nations and provide opportunities for their chess communities to participate in international events. Contact: Email: smallchessnations@gmail.com

item.title: “Theory and Practice of Chess Education” conference begins in Tsaghkadzor
item.dc:creator: editor_d
item.description: Alongside the 2026 World Schools Chess Championship – Europe, the International Scientific Conference “Theory and Practice of Chess Education” officially commenced in Tsaghkadzor, Armenia, running from October 1–2, 2026. Serving as a cornerstone event during this pivotal year for chess education, the conference brought together experts to discuss cutting-edge tools and methodologies. The primary objective is to explore innovative approaches and establish strategies for implementing chess across various educational settings globally. The event opened with inspiring welcome speeches from key leaders in the field. Lilit Mkrtchyan, representing the Armenian State Pedagogical University, welcomed attendees alongside Andrey Vodianov, Chief Operating Officer of the International School Chess Federation (ISCF), who emphasized the mission to “build bridges” globally. Smbat Lputyan, Director of the Chess Scientific Research Institute, outlined the core philosophy of the event by framing chess through its multifaceted lenses of sport, science, education, art, and culture. He highlighted the evolution of the game from a competitive sport into a multidisciplinary field, emphasizing its profound impact on youth development and critical thinking. A major highlight of the conference was the signing of an Official Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between the ISCF, represented by Andrey Vodianov, and the Armenian State Pedagogical University, represented by Lilit Mkrtchyan. This milestone agreement marks a crucial step in turning visionary ideas into practical applications by bridging international chess education initiatives with prestigious academic institutions. Organizers and participants alike expressed great optimism, hoping that this ceremony marks a strong opening for a long, cooperative, and highly successful new era for chess education worldwide.

item.title: WSTC Europe Day 3: Competitions, tactical masterclasses and high-altitude adventures in Tsaghkadzor
item.dc:creator: editor_d
item.description: The third day of the European Continental Stage of the FIDE ISCF World Schools Team Championship 2026 elevated the competitive intensity to new heights in Tsaghkadzor, Armenia. With the tournament crossing into its critical second half, Rounds 5 and 6 delivered a captivating blend of strategic competition on the top boards and heartfelt camaraderie off them. As the top players continued their unstoppable runs, the race for the Grand Final slots became an absolute thriller. The morning air in Tsaghkadzor was crisp, but inside the playing hall where Rounds 5 and 6 of the 2026 FIDE ISCF World Schools Team Championship (European Stage), the atmosphere was white-hot as the tournament leaders finally crossed swords. The penultimate day delivered an extraordinary spectacle of junior chess, showcasing immense fighting spirit, sharp tactical vision, and the brutal reality of time-pressure blunders. With crucial qualification points on the line, the round saw uncompromising chess, with an incredibly low draw rate and an abundance of hard-fought games across all boards. Highlights of Rounds 5 and 6 Gymnasium No. 50 of Minsk (12 Points) holds the top spot after Round 6. Damir Bulgak (Board 1) and Katrina Yakovleva (Board 4) maintain an incredible, perfect 6/6 match record. Riga State Gymnasium No. 1 (10 Points) is firmly in second place. Daniel Beniosev continues his spectacular run on Board 2, sitting on an unbeaten 5.5/6. LEPL Georgia, Kutaisi Andria Razmadze Physico (9 Points) occupies the third position. Their standout performer is Davit Tatvidze, pulling in a vital win today to push his score to 4.5/6. Leading individual board performers The following players have dominated their respective boards across the first six rounds: Tin Biti (OS Spansko Oranice): An exceptional 5.5/6 showing on Board 1. Ioana-Cristiana Pomirleanu (C.N.”Costache Negruzzi”): Dominating Board 4 with a superb 5.5/6 score. Platon Kiritshenko (Tallinna Tonismae Reaalkool): Putting up an elite 5/6 record on Board 3. Let’s have a look at a couple of fragments illustrating the competitive spirit in the event. A real drama unfolded at one of the top boards, in a thrilling game between Gabriel Gabadadze (2071) and Damir Bulgak (2305). Bulgak seized a huge endgame advantage, only to blunder it away with a natural but erroneous 48… Rd2+??, giving White a precious tempo to advance his king. The correct path was 48…Ra5! (or 48…a3!). As played, the position became equal. However, after 49.Kg3 Rd3+ 50.Kh4 a3 51.g5 Rd2 Gabadadze returned the favor by 52.g6?? (instead of the correct 52.Kg3!) and White was losing again. The opponents traded more errors in subsequent play, but eventually Black’s pawns proved to be faster. Ignacy Krol – Troi Krasniqi At first glance, Black has to retreat with his queen, but Krasniqi uncorked 14… Qxg5! – an unexpected queen sacrifice that completely changed the dynamics of the game. After 15.hgx5 Rxh1+ 16.Kd2 Bd7, Black emerged slightly better. Unsettled, Krol reacted poorly and ended up in a lost position. Luckily for him, Krasniqi failed to capitalize, and after a series of mutual errors, the opponents split the point. Fast & local: FIDE-rated girls’ blitz The tournament hall in Tsaghkadzor shifted to a lightning-fast pace on Thursday evening as the International School Chess Federation (ISCF) hosted an official FIDE-rated Blitz Tournament for the young female players under 14 years of age. They were inspired by Elina Danielian, Armenian chess grandmaster and six-time Armenian women’s champion, who assisted in the organization of this tournament. With a time control of 3 minutes plus a 2-second increment, the event “Smart Moves: Girls Who Lead” featured an all-local lineup, bringing together talented young girl-players from Armenia for an evening of intense, high-speed tactical battles. Every match carried high stakes, forcing players to rely on quick intuition and sharp calculation. The evening concluded with rapid handshakes and shared analysis, highlighting the deep pool of local chess talent driving the sport forward. Rising champions Following yesterday’s tradition of high-level educational seminars, the tournament hall hosted another installment of the popular masterclass series. Under the banner “Rising Champions,” coaches, players, and their parents gathered for a deeply practical, interactive conversation with grandmaster Samvel Ter-Sahakyan, Coach of the Japanese National Chess Team for the 2026 Chess Olympiad. The session moved quickly past basic theory, diving straight into the concrete realities of elite youth development. Ter-Sahakyan shared invaluable personal insights on navigating the transition from talented school player to international competitor, emphasizing the psychological resilience needed to bounce back during grueling team tournaments. Mind games beyond the board: WSTC Kahoot Quiz The chess world is incredibly vast, built upon centuries of brilliant minds, legendary rivalries, and a deeply precious history. Capitalizing on this rich heritage, the young prodigies in Tsaghkadzor took a break from their standard calculations to test their historical wits in a fast-paced, interactive Kahoot quiz. The event gave players a fantastic opportunity to showcase their deep knowledge of the game’s greatest milestones and for the winner – to get a postcard signed by five-time World Champion Viswanathan Anand. Captains and parents take the stage: The evening blitz Stepping out from the sidelines and into the competitive arena, team captains and players’ parents had their own opportunity to shine today in a special evening blitz tournament. The friendly yet fiercely contested event gave the adults a taste of the high-pressure environment their children face daily on the top boards. Trading their coaching notes for chess clocks, the participants demonstrated impressive tactical vision and deep passion for the game, proving that the love for chess runs deep across every generation present in Tsaghkadzor. What’s Next? With six rounds down and only two remaining, the European Continental Stage is hurtling toward an epic finale. The team standings are incredibly compressed, and mathematically, nearly a dozen schools are still within striking distance of the podium. Yet, as the kids gathered for dinner, sharing jokes, analyzing games on pocket sets, and teaching each other phrases in different languages, it was beautifully clear that the memories forged in Tsaghkadzor are already the ultimate prize. Official website: https://worldschoolteam2026.fide.com/
